#83034. A tribute to Dean Ashton, the best striker England never had

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Planetfootball ↗ Open Full Page

A tribute to Dean Ashton, the best striker England never had

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Planetfootball

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After shining for Norwich City and West Ham, Dean Ashton became one of England’s big hopes, but a combination of factors meant we never saw the best of the striker for the Three Lions.
  • Every time an England squad is unveiled for a major tournament, we get the inevitable complaints about certain players missing the cut, albeit for different reasons.
  • Occasionally we’ll see complaints that the squad gets packed with established names at the expense of exciting youngsters, while at other times we’ll wind up with younger players from top clubs making the cut ahead of in-form talents from less-fancied clubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After shining for Norwich City and West Ham, Dean Ashton became one of England’s big hopes, but a combination of factors meant we never saw the best of the striker for the Three Lions. It’s a sad ‘what if’ story.

Every time an England squad is unveiled for a major tournament, we get the inevitable complaints about certain players missing the cut, albeit for different reasons.

Occasionally we’ll see complaints that the squad gets packed with established names at the expense of exciting youngsters, while at other times we’ll wind up with younger players from top clubs making the cut ahead of in-form talents from less-fancied clubs.

The latter was certainly the complaint of many when Theo Walcott made the squad for the 2006 World Cup ahead of Darren Bent coming off the back of an impressive season with Charlton.

But there was another player who could feel hard done by: Dean Ashton.

Being overlooked was a recurring theme. In fact, you have to wonder how many more of those predicted future England XIs – which brought notoriety to the likes of Dean Parrett and Patrick Roberts – he’d have featured in had he come through the ranks of a top club’s academy rather than Crewe’s, which was still known for producing top talents but certainly not at the same rate as in the 90s.

However, those who saw him in the early part of his career can attest he was always a special talent.

Indeed, after he left the Cheshire club for Norwich in January 2005 with them in the top half of the Championship, they proceeded to go 18 games without a win and only stayed up on the final day of the season.

Even then, aged just 21, he looked as close as you could get to the complete striker, scoring 20 in 27 games for the Alex and adding seven for a struggling Canaries side after making his top-flight bow.

That tally included a quite lovely volley against Manchester City, the finish of a young man who felt he couldn’t fail with anything he attempted.

Looking at Ashton, most would never have identified him as a man capable of such subtlety, but a lot of that can be put down to England’s specific record with players of his ilk.

The Three Lions have often resisted demanding too much of their frontmen: either giving them the ‘Big man up top’ responsibilities or ensuring they’re nippy with tidy finishing ability – as if anticipating every single pairing should be modelled on the platonic ideal of Niall Quinn and Kevin Phillips.

In fact, going all-in on a combo that was happy with some nice moments and a seventh-place finish does seem quite England, on reflection.

Anyway, by tempering expectations, the sight of a more complete frontman has tended to confuse people, leading to Ashton – even off the back of another great season in 2005-06, overlooked for that summer’s World Cup in Germany.

Indeed, when Walcott was handed a surprise call-up having played no first-team football since January that season, Darren Bent – not Ashton – was the man who many stated should feel hard-done-by.

But while not as prolific as some in that half-season, Ashton was capable of scoring goals you wouldn’t back others to produce – not least his clincher in the FA Cup quarter-final win over Manchester City.

The sight of a hefty striker dancing through a defence with grace and tidy footwork is an underrated genre of goal, like a bear performing ballet, and this was on par with Johan Elmander doing the same for Bolton a few years later.

It revealed Ashton had that touch of class needed to unlock bunched defences, and – with fitness question marks around some of the other squad members that summer – it’s very easy to make retrospective demands for his inclusion with the benefit of a decade’s distance.

Of course, Ashton’s fitness in the summer of 2006 would almost prove ironic given the struggles later in his career, beginning with his first England call-up not long after that World Cup.

An injury in training, following a challenge from Shaun Wright-Phillips, ended up being one from which he never fully recovered, though there was one more hot season – and one stand-out goal – to celebrate before his early retirement in 2009 at the age of just 26.

Ashton’s consolation goal in West Ham’s May 2008 defeat to Manchester United was to overhead kicks what Ashton himself was to No.9s: very different to what we’ve come to expect from the genre, but that doesn’t mean it doesn’t work.

Overhead kicks, generally speaking, can be divided into the Rivaldo-style self-assisted efforts and the side-on excellence produced by the likes of Eidur Gudjohnsen for Chelsea against Leeds United.

Ashton’s was neither of these things, yet the ugly beauty of the finish was a sight to behold.

In a recent development, ashton eyes up the ball like a sniper keeping sight of a moving target, but the process is complicated by his own continued need to readjust. And yet, with the close attentions of Rio Ferdinand and the looming sight of Edwin van der Sar, not once did he seem to consider the prospect of not making a clean contact on the ball.

Sources indicate that would it have been easier to go for a header? Yes. Would it have been more efficient to bring the ball down and beat Van der Sar that way? Almost certainly. Would we be talking about the goal if he’d done either of those things? Heavens no.

Sadly for Ashton, whose one England cap would come that summer, that was pretty much the end of it. He managed just a handful of games the following season before his ankle flared up once more and he made the difficult decision to walk away from the game.

Had England qualified for that summer’s European Championships, he might have been given his chance at a major tournament.

But then again, a healthy Dean Ashton might itself have been enough for England to qualify in the first place.

With England misfiring on more than one occasion in tournaments, conversations invariably turn towards those who played and failed to score. But perhaps we should be talking about the missing piece of the jigsaw who wasn’t there.

So much for Xabi Alonso’s call for cool heads from his Chelsea players. Cole Palmer lost his and was sent off, while goalkeeper Mike Penders punched the ball into his own net to give Tottenham Hotspur a helping hand on their way to a second win at Stamford Bridge in 42 attempts.

This was hardly “the Battle of the Bridge”, but Chelsea blew up during a ridiculous 10-minute spell towards the end of a game in which Tottenham had bossed possession but not looked like scoring.

Palmer was lucky to stay on the pitch in the 70th minute, when he shoved his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes after the Tottenham midfielder had stopped him racing through with a foul and a handball.

Alonso had remarked he was confident his players could keep calm ahead of the game, but he got that wrong – along with his team selection and substitutions.

In between Palmer’s two bookings, Penders suffered his own moment of madness with a bizarre own goal on his league debut for Chelsea. The Belgian was standing in for Emi Martinez, who watched in disbelief from the home dug-out after undergoing surgery on his jaw.

#83032. DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black?
  • Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?
  • Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, you know when you lock your phone and the screen goes black? It seems like it's not doing anything. But it's not doing nothing. It's syncing your messages, updating apps and running other background processes.

Your brain has its own version of that.

Imagine you're sitting on a bus, staring out of a window, taking a shower or walking, and you get that feeling of doing nothing and letting your mind drift?

Well, your mind, the brain, is doing a lot when it feels like you're doing nothing.

It's going over your memories, shaping your sense of who you are, imagining possible futures, helping you understand other people and connecting ideas.

That's your brain's default mode network.

Scientists conducted brain-imaging experiments in the 1990s and early 2000s to find out which regions of the brain were active during demanding tasks, like solving a math problem or memory exercise.

But to measure that, they needed a so-called baseline. They needed to know the level of brain activity at rest and during demanding tasks.

So, between the tasks, they asked participants to relax, close their eyes, stare at a fixed point on a wall, or try not to think of anything at all.

And they measured the participants' brain activity both when they were solving a task and doing nothing. That's how scientists noticed the brain was active in up- and downtime.

They noticed that when participants started to focus on a fresh task, after having done nothing, some brain areas lit up and other areas dimmed down. That suggests those areas that dimmed down must have been active while the participant was apparently — physically and mentally — at rest.

This realization eventually led to the discovery of the default mode network or DMN.

The DMN is crucial because it helps your brain make sense of your life and experiences.

It helps you connect and revisit memories, reflect on who you are, imagine what might happen in future scenarios, understand other people, build meaning from experience, and connect ideas in new ways.

Sources indicate that it turns all your memories, experiences, knowledge, emotions and social information into your internal story. Think of that story as a constantly evolving, updated model of who you are and how you engage with the world around you.

According to recent reports, but it's vital to understand the DMN involves more than one area of the brain. It is a group of brain regions that light up when you're not focused on an external task.

Sources indicate that there's another player in your brain that acts as a monitoring system. You can think of it as constantly asking "Is there anything that needs my attention?".

Imagine you're daydreaming while driving, and a car suddenly swerves into your lane.

In a fraction of a second, your daydream disappears and your attention snaps back to the road. That player is called the salience network, or SN.

The salience network helps you notice key signals, like a sound, a mistake, pain, an emotion, a threat, or something happening in your body, and helps shift the brain toward attention and control systems when action is needed.

The DMN, SN and attention/control systems constantly interact.

And the DMN doesn't just turn off completely with every hard task. Parts of it can also contribute when tasks involve memory, stories, meaning or other people.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

It has been revealed that smartphones have filled many of the small empty moments of our days — waiting for the bus, standing in line, eating alone, lying on the couch. We are constantly looking at our devices.

So, it seems reasonable to ask: are we crowding out those moments of boredom where DMN kicks in?

It has been revealed that maybe. But so far, there's no strong evidence that scrolling directly affects mental health by reducing DMN time.

What we do know is that problematic smartphone use can increase stress, anxiety, task-switching and disrupt sleep.

And sleep loss and stress also have clearer evidence for altering DMN-related brain connectivity.

The DMN is not always necessarily good.

When your mind wanders, it might produce a great fresh idea.

But it might also replay an embarrassing thing you did five years ago. Again. And again.

In depression, the self-reflection part of the DMN can get caught in repetitive negative loops that are hard to stop — what's known as rumination.

According to recent reports, scientists have also found that Alzheimer's disease targets key DMN areas, particularly those responsible for your autobiographical memory and remembering other aspects of the past. Which may help explain why memory problems are so central to the disease.

Protect your sleep and take stress seriously. There is direct evidence that sleep loss and stress disrupt DMN-related connectivity.

In a recent development, take real, quiet breaks after mentally demanding tasks, like studying. It can even help you memorize facts for your exam.

Embrace boredom and enjoy doing nothing.

Try to reframe boredom as this essential, energy-intensive active work in your brain that builds your internal narrative and sense of self, consolidates memories, creates connections and sparks creativity.

Recent findings suggest that try waiting in line without checking your phone. Look out the window next time you take the bus or take a walk without listening to anything.

In a recent development, you can also try scheduling DMN time. It may be the closest thing to a real brain hack.

Published: 05:07 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 05:13 EST, 24 November 2026.

Premier League clubs are bracing themselves for a new raid of their talent from Saudi Arabia, as the mega-money league considers relaxing spending rules.

Teams in the Saudi Pro League (SPL) are presently only allowed eight foreign players in their 25-man squads but are discussing increasing that number to 14 or even higher.

If the move is approved, it is likely to trigger a flood of cash in the market similar to the massive £765million spree in 2023 that saw the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Karim Benzema and N'Golo Kante sign for Public Investment Fund (PIF) teams.

In that 2023 window, almost half of the transfer fees received by Premier League clubs came from the SPL.

In total, 94 players were signed by Pro League clubs and the January transfer window could now follow a similar pattern.

The Saudi spending reached such astronomic levels that it eclipsed every other league in Europe aside from the Premier League.

Cristiano Ronaldo (right) and Angelo, pictured in action for Al Nassr, are among the foreign stars already plying their trade in Saudi Arabia and more will be on their way.

The supposed reason for the proposed rule change is to elevate the standard of existing Saudi players at home by raising the overall level of talent ahead of the country hosting the World Cup in 2034.

But critics argue that the latest rules would only force Saudi players out of their domestic league in place of high-profile foreign recruits.

While Premier League clubs are often reluctant to allow talent to leave in January midway through the season, the fees on offer from Saudi can be eye-watering and hard to turn down.

Aston Villa sold Jhon Duran and later Ollie Watkins for a combined £115million to the SPL.

Fulham accepted £50m for Aleksandar Mitrovic, while Wolves banked £47m for Ruben Neves and Liverpool were able to recoup almost £50m for Darwin Nunez.

West Ham were able to cash in on Crysencio Summerville after relegation last term when Al Hilal bought him for £60m.

In a recent development, would Man United consider offers for Bruno Fernandes as his contract winds down? Or will they keep the club captain to help battle relegation?

Suddenly every Premier League club recruitment department will be reassessing their squads and be keeping a close eye on the rule developments in Saudi.

Ollie Watkins moved from Aston Villa to Al Hilal and the Premier League side have recouped huge fees from the SPL in the  past.

Ivan Toney (second from left) and his Al Ahli team-mates celebrate a goal against Al Nassr.

The SPL's decision on whether to allow the increase of foreign players will be clarified before the winter window opens.

The PIF are winding down their investment in golf through LIV having invested more than £3.7billion since 2021 but their operation in football shows no sign of slowing down.

Players weighing up a move to Saudi will perhaps have a more difficult decision than in 2023 over relocating, with conflict still affecting the country.

The Asian Cup was postponed earlier in November following a missile attack from Yemen-based Houthi rebels on Riyadh airport that killed 13 people and injured more than 300.

Security fears and geo-political uncertainty could make footballers think twice before accepting the lucrative contracts on offer in January and beyond.

  • Neville's dramatic example of Man United's lack of hunger and sharpness came in stark contrast to his pre-season proclamations for the side, when he informed his co-pundit Jamie Carragher that he believed that then-manager Michael Carrick's starting XI was stronger than Liverpool's after a summer recruitment drive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By TAMARA PRENN, SENIOR SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 04:43 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 10:28 EST, 24 November 2026.

Gary Neville showcased the dramatic decline of Manchester United this season as he bizarrely slapped himself in the face on Sky Sports after his former side's 4-0, 10-man, defeat to Liverpool at Anfield.

Neville's dramatic example of Man United's lack of hunger and sharpness came in stark contrast to his pre-season proclamations for the side, when he informed his co-pundit Jamie Carragher that he believed that then-manager Michael Carrick's starting XI was stronger than Liverpool's after a summer recruitment drive.

Instead, Man United saw their numbers reduced inside the opening stages of the game after a reckless challenge by Leny Yoro, and 2-0 down after 13 minutes, with the club legend resorting to drastic methods to convey the side's weaknesses.

Of his old club's defenders, he said: 'I never see any of them on their toes, alert, looking like they've got something fixed in here', before pointing to his head.

Industry observers note that 'I never see any of them look like that,' he added. 'They look like that -'.

Neville then stared into the middle distance for a few moments to share the blankness he sees on the faces of the back line, before spitting: 'Wake up!'.

Gary Neville took to slapping himself to convey the lack of focus he sees in Man United's stars.

The club legend had previously tipped his old side to have a stronger XI than Liverpool's.

But when the two teams met at Anfield, Man United were left woefully exposed after going down to 10 men.

The Overlap broadcaster then slapped his own face a number of times repeating 'wake up!' before adding: 'You play for Man United'.

The gesture left Carragher in stitches, with the Anfield icon collapsing onto the sofa in hysterics - although less impressed with Roy Keane, who displayed his usual sangfroid.

So tickled by the moment was the former Liverpool star that he later changed his profile picture on social media site X to a still image of Neville's hand catching his face.

Neville had more sharp criticism for Man United's defensive selection assessing the inclusion of Matthijs de Ligt in the starting line-up.

The Dutch defender has been out of Premier League action for 51 weeks after suffering a back injury, but was named by Mauricio Pochettino in his first-ever XI.

In a recent development, 'I have a lot of sympathy for him,' Neville admitted. 'It's like playing football after having six pints. It's a strange feeling.

'I have a lot of sympathy for him, it's alarming to watch.'.

Less sympathy for Man United's players came from Keane, who attacked the team - and Neville and Carragher - after the heavy defeat at Anfield confirmed the club's worst start in over 53 years.

The firebrand midfielder was on his usual caustic form as he assessed the damage, hitting out at those who might have accepted the score line, having feared a greater deficit.

Recent findings suggest that 'If I hear that one more time from the lads in the commentary that 4-0 is not too bad when you're down to 10 men - has a team ever got a result with 10 men before?' Keane mentioned immediately after the final whistle. 'It can be done.

According to recent reports, 'I thought United were desperate. I thought they were so bad and everyone and Nev, who played for Man United saying 4-0 ain't bad.'.

In a recent development, '(The red card) doesn't help but you're telling me they couldn't have done better? They lost 4-0 with 10 men, that's not too bad? Has a team ever got a result with 10 men? It can be done. At least show a bit more fight, a bit more quality - I can't believe what I'm hearing from people.

According to recent reports, 'You played for the club, saying 4-0 isn't too bad. Wow. Fans are applauding. Applauding what? Performing rubbish. Liverpool were excellent, but how easy did United make it for them? I can't believe what I'm watching sometimes.

It has been revealed that 'This team two years ago finished 15th. The last year or two, we're talking. We're blaming the board, blaming ownership, blaming managers.

'When do the players take responsibility for some decision-making? Liverpool probably should have scored eight, probably eight or nine, unbelievable chances they had. And everyone's coming off the pitch saying 4 is not too bad? I feel like swearing.'.

Can global leaders put their money where their mouth is on climate?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.
  • "The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he stated, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.
  • Sources indicate that A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The slow international response to climate change has placed the world on a path to destruction, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told heads of state and government during opening statements at this year's COP31 climate conference.

"The ⁠brutal truth is that the climate crisis is outrunning us," he stated, as world leaders gathered in the Turkish resort city of Antalya to set the tone for negotiations at the UN climate summit.

Sources indicate that A UN reportlast month found ​the world will cross a temperature threshold countries agreed to pursue in order to prevent runaway global heating. At the same time, states like Germany are slipping down the rankings for climate action, according to the annual Climate Change Performance Index published Wednesday by New Climate Institute and Germanwatch.

Nonetheless, Guterres said the world has "the power to make sure the overshoot is a temporary breach.".

Negotiators from close to 200 countries are meeting in Turkey at the end of a year characterized by extreme heat waves and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands more missing.

At this year's talks, national representatives are discussing climate solutions such as increasing the share of electricity in an effort to move away from fossil fuels.

On Thursday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, one of the few heads of government from Europe's major economies attending the summit, mentioned that the world's dependence on fossil fuels was at the heart of both the climate crisis and energy security challenges.

"The shift to clean energy is the only route to energy security," he said, endorsing the conference's focus on electrification which he said would lower energy bills, create jobs and protect people from the volatility of fossil fuel markets.

Burnham promised a "new era of British leadership over the next decade," announcing the UK would put climate resilience high on the agenda during its G20 presidency next year.

The US, the world's largest historical emitter of damaging greenhouse gases, is not attending the summit — for the second year in a row after US President Donald Trump withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement in 2025.

Other nations, including major polluters like Germany, France, Italy, Canada and Japan, also opted not to send their top leaders to the talks.

On Wednesday, Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, who is hosting COP31 together with Australia, which is leading negotiations, called on developed nations to take greater responsibility on climate finance.

Financing disagreements center around who should pay for international climate action, whether funding should take the form of grants or loans and how to scale monetary support for developing nations. Many of these countries are among the most vulnerable to the climate crisis but have contributed very little to the emissions causing it.

In a recent development, erdogan said while previous conferences had resulted in different ideas around financing, they have yet to be turned into action. "We set out to make this an implementation COP," he told leaders.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen addressed remarks that developed nations are not contributing enough to climate finance, saying that the transition away from fossil fuels is in "our common interest.".

Recent findings suggest that "Europe is the world's largest provider of climate finance. Last year alone, we contributed more than €32 billion [about $35.5 billion] to support developing countries," she said, adding that Europe will continue to support partners worldwide in tackling climate change.

A recent Carbon Brief analysis found that public funding pledged under the Paris Agreement to help developing countries tackle climate change fell by more than 70% in 2026.

In a recent development, most multi-year pledges from donor countries expired in 2025. Since then, the US has stepped back from international climate efforts, while several European countries have cut their aid budgets, reported Carbon Brief.

Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands in the Pacific, which face an existential threat from rising sea levels, mentioned the response to overshoot "must be overwhelming" and quickly reversed otherwise "the world we know is over.".

"Every fraction of a degree of warming brings more catastrophe," said Heine, adding that more warming makes it more difficult to adapt to living on a hotter planet, brings greater loss and damage from worsening weather extremes and greater financial need.

She called on leaders to triple climate finance by 2035 and make it easier for Small Island Developing States to access the money.

In a recent development, "We are told there is no money, but their spending on war grows; the greatest security threat we face remains underfunded. I appeal to you: Find money for life, not death. Replenish the climate funds," Heine said.

Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese spoke of a "solemn responsibility to this and to future generations ​to act," adding that this is the critical decade.

Australia, the world's third-largest fossil fuel exporter, has vowed to promote the views of the "Pacific family" — small Pacific nations in the region such as Tuvalu or Fiji, where pre-COP meetings were held in October.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Albanese noted it was crucial that climate cooperation delivered practical results — "unlocking investment in clean energy technologies, accelerating electrification, speeding up action for our oceans, unlocking climate finance for those who need it ​most.".

As reasons to speed up electrification von der Leyen pointed to wildfires in Europe and floods in Nepal, as well as droughts stretching from Central America to Sudan, and to the disruption to energy supplies linked to the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.

"The world is witnessing the cost of continuing with the status quo for our climate and our energy security," she noted, adding that the European Union would double down on efforts to become climate neutral.

"Three-quarters ​of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did ​not create and cannot ‌control," UN Secretary-General Guterres stated, adding that recent conflicts have made clear a shift to renewable energy would help improve energy security and the cost-of-living crisis.

Recent findings suggest that von der Leyen also expressed support for COP31's 35-by-35 electrification pledge. The pledge aims to increase electricity's share of final global energy use to 35% by 2035, with von der Leyen saying Europe would be the first "electro-powered" continent.

Heine of the Marshall Islands remarked electrification must must be strictly tied to renewable energy generation rather than fossil fuels, warning that continued oil, coal and gas extraction was a threat to her country's survival.

Sources indicate that iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country wanted compensation for environmental damage caused by US and Israeli strikes, including oil leaks from attacks on tankers. The strikes began in February.

Iran, which is a major fossil fuel producer and has pushed back against strict language on phasing out oil and gas at previous COPs alongside other petrostates, has also struck tankers in the Strait of Hormuz.

Pezeshkian linked the matter to climate finance and said his country expected "responsibility in times of war, to document and assess the environmental damages caused by military aggressions and to develop compensation mechanisms.".

Brazil's President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who hosted last year's COP in the Amazonian city of Belem, remarked the momentum for climate action had dropped off at the start of the year, partly due to the Iran war.

"We started talking more about weapons and tariffs than the survival ‌of future generations," he said.

He also warned that "climate agreements are the favorite targets of reactionary forces at COPs," and urged leaders to work together. Lula promised to protect the Amazon rainforest. "Brazil is back to defend the continuity of a healthy planet," he mentioned.

This article was last updated on November 12 to reflect incoming statements from world leaders.

  • This is a preview of subscription content, access via your institution.
  • Access Nature and 54 other Nature Portfolio journals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, upcoming catalytic manifolds that challenge existing boundaries for synthesis and sustainable manufacturing are notoriously difficult to implement1, particularly for catalytic paradigms based on metals which lack access to the fundamental processes that underpin many established d-block mechanistic pathways (e.g. oxidative addition and reductive elimination). The widespread exploitation of systems based on main-group elements therefore requires alternative elementary steps to effect turnover. Herein, we demonstrate a new catalytic platform for nucleophilic fluorination, which exploits a complex based on calcium (the fifth most Earth-abundant element) as the fluoride delivery vehicle. The key intermediate is a calcium-fluoride complex featuring a terminal Ca–F interaction, a unique structural geometry enabled by a highly sterically encumbered dianionic ligand-scaffold. This intermediate links reactants and products through F– capture and release steps, and thereby unlocks catalytic F– shuttling. Late Ca–F bond breaking in the rate-determining fluoride-delivery transition-state means that electronic and steric tuning of F– by calcium is chemically significant; proof-of-concept results show a hitherto unprecedented level of selectivity for substitution over elimination brought about by Ca-modulation. In a broader context, this work demonstrates how control over catalyst speciation and reagent binding affinity are key factors for the future development of sustainable non-transition metal paradigms in catalysis.

#83025. Industry News: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1039 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1039 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.
  • For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.
  • It has been revealed that in late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.

It has been revealed that in late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.

The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.

Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.

However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.

The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that this is "only part of the story.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.

The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.

Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it stated.

According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts.".

But critics see this as a major weakness.

"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.

Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects. For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

Sources indicate that for 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly crucial documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement intends, vary widely or are missing entirely," stated Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond promptly and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, remarked the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough.".

Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he mentioned, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.

In a recent development, criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not newly introduced. A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.

The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.

For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she noted.

According to recent reports, as of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

According to recent reports, but Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles.".

The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive.".

The new rules have been in effect for only 10 months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.

Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.

Recent findings suggest that such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said. However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.

The bank stated that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns.".

"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.

Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards.".

This article was originally written in German.

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Mauricio Pochettino suggested the Leny Yoro red card that had such an affect ontheir defeat by Liverpool game was 'unfair' and that their opponents should have been 'punished' too.

Sources indicate that 'We are not going to lose more than one game how we lost today. I take the responsibility, and we keep pushing.

Manchester United boss Mauricio Pochettino blamed Leny Yoro's red card for his side's defeat by Liverpool.

A quick sprint, a well-placed pass and an instinctive finish. Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak will have done this dozens of times in training but here, on a squally Sunday afternoon, this combination secured a little piece of history.

Liverpool invested a near quarter-billion pounds on Barcola and Isak for bigger occasions than a tussle with Brighton and Hove Albion, but this rapid interchange felt like a significant moment.

Liverpool are a work in progress under Andoni Iraola but with each minute of each game you can see signs of things knitting together, and if Barcola and Isak are finding harmony, with Florian Wirtz in behind, then, perhaps, this journey will start to accelerate.

This was an important afternoon for Liverpool’s head coach, a difficult assignment against high-flying, well-respected opponents in Brighton, who arrived on Merseyside having won their last four Premier League fixtures with a combined aggregate of 15-0, including a 3-0 thumping of reigning champions Arsenal.

But Liverpool rose impressively to the challenge and there are grounds for saying this was the most significant success to date for Iraola, whose team defended relentlessly to preserve a clean sheet. They are up to fourth now after this 2-0 success and deserve their position.

“I’m very happy,” Iraola mentioned. “We faced a very good opponent, similar to Villarreal [in the Champions League]. It’s difficult to defend them a lot of times and it was key how we started. We needed to be aggressive, recover balls, win our duels, be dangerous in transitions: I think we’ve done it.”.

Recent findings suggest that and how. Iraola was able to march towards the Kop at the end, to clap the supporters and acknowledge only Liverpool’s fifth (and his first) Premier League win at Anfield in 2026, and it was evident he had a spring in his step from what he had seen.

Whether the game would have flowed in the direction it did had Brighton taken the lead can only be speculated but what a glorious chance they wasted for us to find out: in the 13th minute, five swift, one-touch passes bamboozled Liverpool’s defence and created space for Yasin Ayari.

With the goal at his mercy, Ayari could have made things exceptionally uncomfortable but he leant back and blazed over. He clasped his face and grimaced, knowing what had gone begging in front of the Kop; four minutes later, his misery was exacerbated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Moyes was presented with a commemorative frame ahead of Monday night’s Premier League away fixture against Brentford – a record-breaking match for the Everton manager.

The trip to the Gtech Community Stadium will mark Moyes’ 593rd game as Everton manager, taking him ahead of the legendary Harry Catterick in the all-time rankings.

Everton captain James Tarkowski and former Blues midfielder Leon Osman were on hand to present the signed frame – and Moyes said it’s a “privilege and honour” to have reached the historic milestone.

Sources indicate that "I'm really thrilled about. I've become the manager who has managed more Everton games than anyone before. That's a privilege and an honour to be put in that position.

"I have to thank the people who brought me to the Club in the first place. When you take a chance on a young manager, you never know it'll be work, but they had great faith and believed in me.

"I'm so thankful for the people around Everton because they've been so good for me.".

Handing over the frame, Osman remarked: “It’s a record I don’t think will ever be beaten – and I don’t say that lightly. This is some achievement for a huge football club.

Industry observers note that “I’m sure James is like me in saying it’s been an honour to play for you. It’s been an honour, a privilege. It’s been hard! But you’ve made us all better and we wish you many more successes for the upcoming seasons.”.

Industry News: Intelligent women get less help at work, study finds

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (729 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that high intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work.
  • Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often.
  • The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that high intelligence is usually counted as an asset at work. But a new study suggests that for women, it can also lead to worse treatment from colleagues.

Across 826 people in the United States and China, women who scored higher on an intelligence test were rated by their teammates as more hostile, received less help and were undermined more often. Men with high scores did not receive such treatment, and in one group, they were treated better.

The study examined whether people's cognitive ability affects how their teammates treat them and whether that differs between women and men.

Since it was published this year, Nitya Chawla, an associate professor at UCL School of Management in London and the researcher behind the study, indicates women have written to her saying the findings matched their own experience at work. Some told her they had wondered whether they were to blame for hostility.

Industry observers note that the researchers ran two studies. The first followed 432 business students at a US public university working in small teams on a consulting project for real organizations. The second surveyed 394 full-time employees working in teams at a financial tech giant in China.

Intelligence here means cognitive ability measured with a standardized test of reasoning and problem-solving that employers use in hiring. Teammates were not told of anyone's scores. They rated one another, and a few weeks later each person reported how much help they had received and how often they had been undermined, for instance by having information withheld.

According to recent reports, the effects were small, and the study shows a link, not proof that colleagues' perceptions caused the treatment. Participants reported help and mistreatment themselves, and the study did not look at race or ethnicity.

In the student group, the difference between women and men was no longer statistically significant when two participants with extremely low scores were included.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In a recent development, the researchers point to social role theory, the idea that people expect men and women to fit traditional roles: men as capable and assertive, women as warm and supportive. A woman with high cognitive ability breaks that expectation, and colleagues may assume she lacks warmth.

"It's that automatic, implicit assumption that takes place alongside the presence of intelligence that then drives these more negative interpersonal behaviors," Chawla told DW.

Sources indicate that in both groups, women with higher scores were rated as more hostile. Among the employees in China, they were also rated as less warm. Women seen as more hostile reported less help, both with their work and on a personal level, and more undermining.

Industry observers note that the team also checked whether the women were simply behaving differently. Higher-scoring women were rated as somewhat more domineering, but that did not explain why they received less help or more mistreatment. The findings point to colleagues' assumptions, Chawla claims, rather than to anything the women did.

No, men with high intelligence scores do not face the same treatment. Among the students in the United States, a man's score made no difference to how his teammates rated or treated him.

It has been revealed that among the employees in China, men with higher scores were rated as less hostile, received more help and were mistreated less often. The authors suggest the difference between the two groups may reflect cultural differences in gender norms, but they did not test this.

Sources indicate that no, Chawla indicates. "That would be really the wrong conclusion to draw.".

It has been revealed that small effects still matter, she argues, because they are experienced day after day. Over time, this kind of treatment can lead to anxiety, self-doubt and a sense of not belonging. "These experiences and these feelings can become very, very burdensome over time," she said.

According to recent reports, chawla puts the responsibility on workplaces rather than on women. Managers, she says, should track how team members treat one another, and organizations should hold regular check-ins to see whether employees are getting equal support.

Individuals can ask themselves a simple question, she notes: would they react the same way if that colleague were a man?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (297 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026.
  • Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026.
  • It has been revealed that the authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Original Article was published on 24 June 2026.

Retraction to: Nature https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10702-5 Published online 24 June 2026.

It has been revealed that the authors retract this article, following a suggestion from the editors. Shortly after publication, a preprint (subsequently published (see ref. 1 below)) by Till Sawala identified an inconsistency in our analysis. Our calculations were erroneously comparing the comoving distance between the observed galaxies to the luminosity distance between galaxies in the simulated mocks. Correcting these concerns reduces the discrepancy between the observed and simulated samples to 1.48–2.75 sigma, depending on the sample construction. This falls below the standard significance threshold of 3 sigma in the cosmology literature.

Recent findings suggest that despite the revised uncertainties, our method remains valid and provides tentative evidence for anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of galaxies in the Universe. The revised paper, with corrected uncertainties, will be submitted to another journal. This retraction will contain a link to the newly introduced publication, if and when it is published.

Both authors agree with this retraction.

By LEWIS BROWNING, SPORTS REPORTER.

Published: 12:23 EST, 22 November 2026 | Updated: 10:28 EST, 24 November 2026.

Gary Neville led the criticism of Manchester United's defending in the opening minutes against Liverpool as Mauricio Pochettino's reign started in disastrous fashion at Anfield.

After just eight minutes, his intends were thrown into tatters when errors from Matthijs de Ligt and Leny Yoro saw the latter sent off before Liverpool took a swift lead.

A long ball from Ronald Araujo should have been dealt with easily by De Ligt, but the Dutchman found himself in no man's land, left the ball, and Alexander Isak raced clear.

That left Yoro scrambling to try to recover the situation for his side, but Isak stepped across him and he ended up fouling the Reds forward.

Referee Sam Barrott wasted no time in pulling out the red card, and United found themselves reduced to 10 men just minutes into a vital clash.

And former United defender Neville didn't hold back when it came to his analysis as he tore into the two players at fault.

Recent findings suggest that leny Yoro is SENT OFF after eight minutes! 😱 pic.twitter.com/VKYvckvBBP.

Gary Neville torn into Manchester United duo Leny Yoro (right) and Matthijs de Ligt after the former was sent off.

Neville (pictured) questioned why the duo were playing as if they had 'never had basic training of how to play in defence'.

In a recent development, 'When I saw De Ligt's name on the team sheet I have to admit I was absolutely stunned,' he stated, speaking on Sky Sports. 'And the reason I was stunned was because of this. If you'd watched him in Como four weeks ago he was very much well off it and that is just a basic ball over the top.

Recent findings suggest that 'It's his problem to start with, Yoro can be further across, but De Ligt is miles away from it, then Yoro has to get further round, he reacts late, his anticipation is poor. It's so clumsy from Yoro, he makes a lot of these types of mistakes.

'You could argue Isak delays to make sure Yoro runs into him, but it's naivety.'.

Pochettino was left scrambling to think of ideas to tighten up the defence but, before he could bring Harry Maguire on, it was 2-0 through Florian Wirtz.

Maguire eventually came on but it felt like too little, too late.

According to recent reports, 'We saw him in Como and he has been out for a year,' Neville continued on De Ligt. 'It is really tough to come back. To have him out there in a game like this, he has been exposed. Yoro's positioning is poor, he has to be across, you have to cover your mate. It is bad all around from United.

'Michael Carrick will be watching and say that's what I was having to deal with.'.

And his criticism didn't stop there. After having the chance to re-watch the incident, Neville's criticism grew even stronger.

De Ligt (left) failed to deal with a long ball as Alexander Isak (right) raced away before the foul.

Former United captain Roy Keane (pictured) added that he was 'amazed' by the errors made.

Industry observers note that 'It's as bad defending from two centre backs defending a long ball as you will see,' the former defender, who likened a return from a year out to playing after six pints of alcohol, added. 'De Ligt is well out of it - he's been out so I have some sympathy. But between them, to let the ball beat you, it's unforgivable.

'It is shocking. Whilst Man United have those types of defenders in their team, they have no chance of keeping a clean sheet.

Sources indicate that 'It's basic understanding of how to play a position. It's the fundamentals. It's like these guys have never had basic training of how to play in defence.'.

Former United captain Roy Keane chimed in too, adding at half-time: 'It doesn't matter if it's a back four or back five, you do the basics right.

It has been revealed that 'I'm amazed at this level, I know he's been out a while, but it's really poor defending. He's never getting that ball.

'If you're a defender you always expect the worst. Isak's done well and I actually don't think he's going to get the ball.

'There's no way he's (Yoro) getting the ball, it's clumsy by United. Straight ball over the top and he's in big trouble. But there's no way he's getting that ball. I know he's quick and sharp but it's really poor defending. Players not smelling danger.'.

#83016. What are fossil fuels?

What are fossil fuels?

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life.
  • The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.
  • It has been revealed that they started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether in the form of crumbly rock, odorless gas or slick black liquid, ancient organic compounds have powered the flourishing of modern life. But now they threaten to make the planet unlivable for many plants, animals and humans.

The collective term refers to coal, oil and natural gas — a group of energy sources that contain carbon and hydrogen.

It has been revealed that they started life hundreds of millions of years ago as living plants and animals. When they died, they sank to the bottom of oceans and swamps where they decomposed under layers of sediment.

Over time, this matter was buried deeper and deeper into the earth, subjecting it to increasing pressure and heat which changed its chemical composition. Plants and trees transformed into coal, whereas microscopic plankton and algae became oil and — if the heat and pressure increased further — gas.

Today fossil fuels can be found in the earth's crust all around the world although some countries, such as the US, Saudi Arabia and Russia, have bigger reserves than others.

Coal, found in underground coal beds, is extracted by mining, whereas oil and gas, found in reservoirs beneath the land and ocean, are accessed by drilling.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Since the early 19th Century, when the discovery and exploitation of fossil fuel reserves powered the Industrial Revolution, our use of them has skyrocketed, increasing eight-fold since 1950.

Today they provide 80% of our energy needs through heating, electricity generation and transport.

We transform them into energy either by burning them directly in furnaces that warm up our homes and businesses, or in power plants to heat water into steam which then generates electricity. When it comes to transport, crude oil is refined into a range of products such as diesel, gasoline and kerosene that are burned in the engines of automobiles, airplanes and ships. Natural gas is also sometimes compressed for use in cars and buses.

But fossil fuels are also essential to a huge range of products including steel, formed using a coal-derived material called coke, and plastic, which is produced by refining and processing crude oil and gas.

According to recent reports, fossil fuels are by far the biggest contributors to climate change. When burned to power our modern lives, they emit carbon dioxide (CO2) into Earth's atmosphere, trapping heat and causing temperatures to rise.

With 2025 officially one of the warmest years on record, the impact of these emissions is being felt around the world. Hotter temperatures are causing polar ice caps to melt and creating the conditions for extreme weather events — such as floods, drought, wildfires and storms — to become more intense and frequent.

Recent findings suggest that scientists stress the need to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) to avoid unleashing the most catastrophic impacts of climate change. That was laid out in the 2015 Paris Agreement. Currently, there are 194 parties to the agreement, but progress has been too slow, and overall emissions continue to rise.

Recent findings suggest that three years after countries agreed at the UN climate conference in Dubai COP28 to transition away from coal, oil and gas. After the previous COP in Brazil failed to reach a consensus on a concrete proposal, Brazil has now presented a roadmap aimed at turning that promise into national intends.

"It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable," United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres noted.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Has there been a better goalkeeper in the Premier League this season than Leeds United’s James Trafford? It is a question worth asking after his brilliance secured his side a point against Sunderland.

Opinions will vary, of course, but the body of evidence to back Trafford’s argument to permanently dislodge Jordan Pickford as England No 1 looked even stronger at the Stadium of Light.

In a recent development, after leaving Manchester City in the summer to play regularly following a frustrating season as backup, Trafford is proving to be a brilliant buy for Leeds. He is the most expensive British goalkeeper. More importantly, he is playing like it too.

Sources indicate that this was a tough examination for Leeds, who were not at their best, against a typically robust and physically challenging Sunderland who are getting back to doing the things that made them so difficult to play against last season. Regis Le Bris’ side created the better chances but were repeatedly denied by Trafford.

With the windy weather playing havoc, ruining the game as a spectacle, as both sides struggled for control of the ball, the two moments of quality came from Trafford in the first half.

In a recent development, goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

Industry observers note that the first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

Sources indicate that the second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

In a recent development, trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Robin Roefs is at it again with another key save for Sunderland 👏 https://t.co/SJ4qWmSHBo.

Had the former Newcastle United player scored so late in the game, the home crowd’s frustration may have boiled over. The point means Le Bris’ side have still not won a league game since August and remain bottom of the table. This is proving to be a tougher second season in the top flight for Sunderland, but if they keep playing like this, they will not remain in the bottom three for much longer.

“It’s a positive [point],” said Le Bris. “The more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.”.

“It’s a positive [point], the more positive [thing] is the way we played with intensity, togetherness - we were Sunderland today.

According to recent reports, “It’s still a long journey, we know with this busy schedule playing in Europe, playing in the Carabao Cup, it’s a upcoming challenge for us and we need to embrace it. I think we demonstrated this afternoon that we are in this challenge, we want to embrace it and be ourselves and we probably deserved a bit more today.”.

“I think it was a good effort from everybody so obviously we want three points from where we are in the table but keep putting up the performances like that and we’ll get some.

“As a defender it’s always nice to have a clean sheet and especially after the last few games where we haven’t had one.

“It’s always something we’re looking to do and Robin [Roefs] came up with some major saves, Omar [Alderete] coming on was really good as well and I hope my teammate’s [Nordi Mukiele] OK as well because I think that was kind of my fault. But we got the clean sheet for him so hopefully not too bad.”.

When asked about Sunderland being bottom of the league, he replied: “I think always the table reflects fairly where teams deserve to be, and I think over the course of the course of the season if we keep putting in performances like that it will represent where we should be.

“But the table always reflects where people should be but we need to keep looking at ourselves, don’t look at other anyone else, it’s no-one else’s fault but us and we know that.”.

That result means that Sunderland’s stay bottom of the Premier League and without a win in the competition since August 30, while Leeds earn their fifth draw in eight top-flight fixtures to move up to seventh on 11 points.

Ampadu’s cross finds its way to Okafor, who helps the ball into the danger zone towards Longstaff. The midfielder shoots from close range, but Sunderland throw in a couple of bodies to block it.

Sunderland were warned about “second season syndrome” and shrugged them off in the summer as they looked forward to their first European campaign for more than 50 years.

They had dismissed the gloomy pre-season predictions the previous year and had gone on to enjoy their most successful season in the top flight since the heady days of the Peter Reid era at the start of the century.

The final game of this gameweek sees these two Northern giants lock horns once again in a very intriguing encounter, with Sunderland especially in need of three points.

It has been revealed that following their opening season back in the Premier League last term, Sunderland enjoyed a historic campaign, placing seventh to qualify for European competition for the first time in 53 years. Therefore, their workload for the 2025-26 season has increased, which has caused their domestic form to suffer.

Recent findings suggest that sunderland presently find themselves bottom of the top-flight table, with just one win and four points from their opening seven league matches. They’ve lost their previous four Premier League games, but a win here could lift them out of the drop zone, depending on other results at Old Trafford and Selhurst Park.

In a recent development, meanwhile, in the Europa League, it’s a completely different story. Regis Le Bris’ side are unbeaten, earning seven points from the first nine available. They drew 1-1 with Polish outfit Lech Poznan on Thursday evening, and given the relentless juggling act of domestic and European football, they’re already back in today against a very well-drilled team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.
  • In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
  • The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier said Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The Upcoming York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

It has been revealed that megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

In a recent development, kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who at the moment works in the firm's robotics division.

Rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Industry observers note that nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the firm and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," remarked Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank.

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole company behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the firm for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the organization so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

At the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The firm has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is quickly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The issue is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Everton saw only their second loss at Goodison Park this season in a narrow 1-0 defeat to Brighton in the WSL on Sunday afternoon.

Coming off the back of a three-game unbeaten streak against a trio of top teams of the division, the Blues struggled to take the edge in Sunday’s showdown with the Seagulls.

In the first ten minutes, Brighton’s aggressive pressing pushed the Blues’ backline and forced an error of miscommunication, giving them an early lead.

The next 80 minutes saw the Toffees battle it out to take back control on home ground, but ultimately, they couldn’t find the back of the opposition’s net.

Head Coach Scott Phelan’s line-up was rotated from the team that took on Manchester United in the Subway Players Cup showdown in midweek with Courtney Brosnan in net, a fresh backline and Ruby Mace and Yuka Momiki starting.

According to recent reports, after the early concession, Brosnan was called in to action once more to deny Kiko Seike. The forward latched on to a threaded through ball and stabbed at goal, with the Republic of Ireland international standing her ground to deny the visitors a quick second.

On the other end of the pitch, Noemie Mouchon and Momiki took turns to test the Seagulls’ defence, but neither chances could escape Brighton’s Chiamaka Nnadozie in goal.

That concluded the action for the first 45, with both sides battling to take what felt like an imminent second goal of the match, but neither found the back of the net.

Substitutions for the second half saw Jutta Rantala come on for Mouchon at the break.

Just three minutes after the whistle, Everton forward Ornella Vignola received a narrow cross from Momiki just outside of the box. She sent a powerful strike slightly wide of the goal, much to Brighton’s luck.

Industry observers note that the Seagulls retaliated with a furious counter-attack. That was no match for Brosnan’s reflexes that guided striker Seike’s shot onto the post, and away from the back of the net.

According to recent reports, the remainder of the second half saw a more dangerous side of the Toffees, with Vignola and Rantala both going one-on-one with Brighton’s defence in the 60th and 66th minute after balls from midfield powerhouse Ruby Mace. Yet despite their best efforts, there was still no goal.

With 68 minutes gone, Phelan looked for fresh legs and took off makeshift winger Maz Pacheco for Hannah Cain.

It has been revealed that in the 76th minute, another chance fell to Hikaru Kitagawa. This time, the Japanese defender broke through midfield up the left wing and came head-to-head with Brighton’s defence. But, her efforts came to a close when she was faced with pressure and volleyed the ball sharply over the crossbar.

Immediately afterwards, final changes were made to the team, with Aurora Galli coming on for Hannah Blundell.

In a recent development, the action-packed second half came to a final showdown in the 85th minute. Seike crossed to Marisa Olislagers who was waiting outside the box. The Dutch midfielder pelted the ball towards the Toffees' net, but it was met by Brosnan who in yet another odds-defying save, punched the ball over the crossbar to the Seagulls' despair.

Late offences saw the Toffees win two corners, but the Blues were still unable to penetrate Arturo Ruiz’s goal line in a series of struggles in the box.

The final whistle blew and the game came to an end – the affair decided by the unfortunate own goal inside six minutes.

Everton will next play Arsenal at home in the WSL on Friday 11 December. Until then the squad will break off to play in a series of international friendlies.
